en.title: Prayer Time Explanations
en.intro: Detailed explanations of the prayer-time and timetable markers used by Proud Muslim.
en.note: These are prayer boundaries and timetable conventions, not eighteen separate obligatory prayers. Juristic boundaries may differ by madhhab and calculation authority.
shortTexts: Imsak begins at true dawn. The Fajr period and the fast begin at this point; fasting users must stop eating and drinking before the displayed time.
The Fajr prayer period begins at Imsak and ends at sunrise. This later Sabah marker is a cautious timetable recommendation, not a second legal dawn.
Sunrise ends the Fajr period and begins a prohibited prayer interval. The warning remains active until the sun has clearly risen at Ishraq.
Ishraq marks the end of the sunrise prohibition after the sun has risen clearly above the horizon. Voluntary morning prayer may then be offered.
Dahve-i Kübrâ is halfway between Imsak and sunset. In Hanafi fasting law it affects the latest intention time for certain current-day or voluntary fasts.
This brief red warning surrounds solar noon, when the sun reaches its highest point. Avoid beginning prayer until the interval ends and Dhuhr starts.
Dhuhr begins after the sun crosses the meridian and shadows lengthen again. It continues until the applicable Asr boundary selected by the user.
This is the first-shadow Asr boundary used by the Shafi‘i, Maliki and Hanbali schools and by Abu Yusuf and Muhammad within the Hanafi school.
This later two-shadow Asr boundary is attributed to Imam Abu Hanifa. It is an alternative calculation for the same Asr prayer, not another prayer.
Isfirar begins when the sun yellows near sunset. Do not delay Asr without excuse; if it remains unperformed, pray its obligatory units before sunset.
Maghrib begins when the sun has completely set. Its period continues until the applicable twilight boundary for Isha, though prompt performance is preferred.
Ishtibak marks the stage when stars become clearly numerous. It warns against delaying Maghrib this late without a valid reason and is not another prayer.
This first Isha marker begins when red twilight disappears. It is used by three Sunni schools and by Abu Yusuf and Muhammad in the Hanafi school.
This later Isha marker begins when the remaining white twilight disappears and is attributed to Imam Abu Hanifa. It is not a second Isha prayer.
Islamic midnight is halfway from Maghrib to the next Imsak, so it is not necessarily 12:00 a.m. It is relevant to juristic limits on delaying Isha.
Tahajjud is voluntary night prayer. This timetable marks the final third of the legal night, a valued period for prayer, supplication and forgiveness.
Sahar is the last sixth of the legal night before Imsak. It is valued for prayer, remembrance, forgiveness and eating suhur before a fast.
Qibla Time uses the sun’s calculated alignment with the Qibla bearing. Follow the displayed front, side or back instruction and never look directly at the sun.
longTexts: Imsak means the beginning of true dawn (*al-fajr al-sadiq*), when horizontal light begins to spread along the eastern horizon. From this point, the legal night ends, the Fajr prayer period begins, and a person observing a fast must abstain from food, drink, and anything else that invalidates the fast. A timetable may show a separate later “Fajr/Sabah” recommendation for congregational or precautionary practice, but this does not create a second beginning for the obligatory prayer. Calculation authorities may use different solar-depression angles or safety adjustments, especially at high latitudes; the app must therefore show the active calculation method.

Fajr is the first obligatory prayer of the day. Its legal period begins with true dawn, shown as Imsak, and ends when the sun begins to rise. In the supplied timetable convention, “Sabah” appears 15-20 minutes after Imsak as a cautious recommended time for performing the prayer. It should be presented as a timetable recommendation rather than as a second legal dawn. Users must still understand that delaying Fajr until sunrise would take the prayer outside its prescribed period. Local mosque congregation times may differ from both Imsak and the displayed recommendation.

The Sunrise marker is the calculated moment when the upper edge of the sun appears above the observer's visible horizon. It marks the end of the Fajr prayer period. Voluntary prayer should not be initiated while the sun is rising; the red Kerahat warning remains active until the sun has risen sufficiently, which this timetable identifies with the Ishraq marker. Terrain, elevation, atmospheric refraction, and the difference between a mathematical and visible horizon may affect observed sunrise, so users should follow the selected authoritative timetable for worship.

Ishraq is a timetable marker showing that the sun has risen far enough for the sunrise prohibition to end. In the supplied convention, this occurs when the sun is approximately a spear's height above the visible horizon, represented astronomically by the sun's centre being about 5 degrees above the true horizon. The voluntary morning prayer offered near the beginning of this period is commonly called Ishraq; it also falls within the broader Duha period. Because the precise number of minutes after sunrise changes with latitude, season, and calculation rules, the app should use the computed Ishraq value rather than a fixed delay.

Dahwa al-Kubra, sometimes called the greater forenoon, is the midpoint of the legal daytime measured from Imsak to sunset; it occurs before solar noon. It is primarily a fasting-related timetable marker, not a prayer. In Hanafi jurisprudence it is relevant to the last time by which an intention may be made for certain fasts, including a current Ramadan fast, a specified vow, or a voluntary fast, provided no act invalidating the fast has occurred since dawn. Make-up, expiatory, and unspecified vowed fasts require intention before dawn. Other madhhabs may formulate intention rules differently, so the popup should identify this as school-specific guidance.

The midday Kerahat period surrounds solar culmination, when the sun reaches its highest daily position and is about to cross the local meridian. Prophetic guidance identifies the interval at the height of midday until the sun begins to decline as a time in which prayer should not be performed. The supplied timetable applies a precautionary interval before Dhuhr; for its Istanbul convention, the start is described as two precaution units, totalling about 20 minutes, before the displayed Dhuhr time. This duration is a timetable convention and must be computed from the selected data source rather than globally hardcoded. The card and main prayer page should show a red warning until Dhuhr begins.

Dhuhr is the obligatory noon prayer. Its period begins after the sun crosses the local meridian and the shortest shadow of the day begins to lengthen. Its ending boundary depends on the Asr rule being followed. Under the first-shadow rule, associated with Abu Yusuf, Muhammad al-Shaybani, and the other three Sunni madhhabs, Asr begins when an object's added shadow equals its height. Under the two-shadow rule attributed to Abu Hanifa, Asr begins when the added shadow reaches twice the object's height. The noon shadow already present at culmination is excluded from both measurements. Proud Muslim should display the user's selected school or calculation setting clearly.

The first-shadow Asr marker begins when an object's shadow, excluding its noon shadow, becomes equal to the object's height. It is the standard Asr boundary in the Shafi'i, Maliki and Hanbali schools and is also attributed to Abu Yusuf and Muhammad al-Shaybani within the Hanafi school. In the supplied timetable it is shown as the primary “Asr” time. Users following Abu Hanifa's two-shadow position may instead use the later Asr al-Thani marker. This marker changes with latitude, date, and solar position; it is not produced by simply adding a fixed number of minutes to Dhuhr.

Asr al-Thani means the second Asr boundary. It begins when an object's added shadow, excluding the shadow present at solar noon, reaches twice the object's height. This position is attributed to Imam Abu Hanifa and is widely used in Hanafi prayer timetables. It does not represent another prayer; it provides an alternative juristic calculation for when the same obligatory Asr period begins. Proud Muslim should allow the selected fiqh setting to determine which Asr marker is primary while still explaining the alternative. The displayed time must be calculated astronomically for the user's location and date.

Isfirar al-Shams describes the late-afternoon stage when the sun becomes yellow and nears the horizon. The supplied convention places its start when the sun's centre is approximately 5 degrees above the true horizon and continues until sunset. Prophetic reports identify the yellowing of the sun as the end of Asr's preferred period and prohibit seeking voluntary prayer as sunset approaches. Deliberately delaying Asr to this stage without excuse is blameworthy. A person who has not yet performed Asr should nevertheless perform the obligatory prayer before sunset rather than knowingly let it become missed. The app should display a red Kerahat indicator throughout this interval.

Maghrib is the obligatory sunset prayer. Its period begins after the sun's disk has completely disappeared below the local visible horizon. It continues until twilight disappears, although the definition of the relevant twilight boundary differs among juristic opinions. The prayer is generally performed promptly after sunset. Proud Muslim should not treat a phone's clock or a visually obstructed horizon as sufficient evidence by itself; it should use the selected authoritative calculation and location. The later Ishtibak marker warns against unnecessarily delaying Maghrib until stars have become prominent under the supplied timetable convention.

Ishtibak al-Nujum refers to the stage after sunset when the stars become clearly numerous or intermingled in the darkening sky. In the supplied convention, it corresponds approximately to the sun reaching 10 degrees below the visible horizon; around Istanbul, the interval after sunset varies through the year. This is a timetable warning associated with delaying Maghrib, not the start of another obligatory prayer. The exact religious characterization and exceptions should be reviewed for each madhhab. Because the interval varies by season and latitude, the app must use the day's calculated marker rather than a fixed number of minutes after Maghrib.

The supplied timetable labels the first Isha boundary as Isha al-Awwal. It occurs when the red twilight in the western sky disappears. The document represents this with the sun's upper edge at approximately 17 degrees below the visible horizon. This boundary is attributed to Abu Yusuf and Muhammad al-Shaybani and is used by the other three Sunni madhhabs. The precise depression angle adopted by modern prayer-time organizations can differ; consequently, the displayed value must come from the selected calculation authority. Users following Abu Hanifa's later white-twilight position may use Isha al-Thani.

Isha al-Thani is the second, later twilight marker. It occurs when the remaining white glow in the western sky disappears after the red twilight has already gone. The supplied timetable represents this with the sun's upper edge approximately 19 degrees below the visible horizon and attributes this beginning of Isha to Imam Abu Hanifa. It is an alternative juristic boundary for the same obligatory Isha prayer, not a separate prayer. At high latitudes twilight may persist or disappear abnormally, requiring a recognized high-latitude method; the app should state which adjustment is active.

Islamic midnight is calculated by measuring the legal night from Maghrib to the following Imsak and dividing that duration in half. The midpoint is then added to Maghrib. It therefore changes daily and normally does not coincide with civil midnight. Sahih Muslim describes Isha's time in relation to half the night. Jurists differ over whether this point is the final valid boundary or the end of the preferred period in particular circumstances. The supplied document notes a Shafi'i view treating the halfway point as Isha's end and describes delay beyond it as disliked in the Hanafi school. This entry should be presented as guidance requiring madhhab-aware wording.

Tahajjud is voluntary prayer performed during the night, commonly after sleeping. The supplied timetable marks Tahajjud when two-thirds of the legal night have passed, meaning the final third has begun. It continues until Imsak. The Qur'an encourages additional prayer during the night, and an authentic hadith gives special importance to supplication and seeking forgiveness during the last third. This marker identifies a recommended opportunity, not a new obligatory prayer period. The supplied source also advises that a person with missed obligatory prayers should give priority to fulfilling obligatory duties; detailed prioritization should follow the user's school and qualified guidance.

Sahar is the closing portion of the night immediately before true dawn. In the supplied timetable it is calculated as the final one-sixth of the legal night between Maghrib and Imsak. The Qur'an praises those who seek forgiveness before dawn, and this quiet period is traditionally used for supplication, remembrance, recitation, and preparation for fasting. The pre-dawn meal is called suhur. Sahar ends when Imsak begins; a fasting person should therefore finish eating and drinking before the displayed Imsak boundary rather than treating sunrise as the deadline.

Qibla Time is an astronomical direction-finding aid. The Qibla bearing is the great-circle direction from the selected location toward the Kaaba. At a calculated time, the sun's azimuth aligns with that direction or with a defined right-angle or opposite relationship. Depending on geography, the correct instruction may be to face the sun, place it on the right or left, or keep it behind. Therefore, Proud Muslim must display the computed instruction together with the time; it must not universally tell every user to face the sun. Buildings, blocked horizons, and unsafe viewing conditions must also be considered. Never look directly at the sun; use a shadow line where practical.

tr.title: Namaz Vakitlerinin Açıklamaları
tr.intro: Proud Muslim’da kullanılan namaz vakitleri ve takvim işaretlerinin ayrıntılı açıklamaları.
tr.note: Bunlar namaz sınırları ve takvim işaretleridir; on sekiz ayrı farz namaz değildir. Fıkhî sınırlar mezhep ve hesaplama kurumuna göre değişebilir.
shortTexts: İmsâk, fecr-i sâdıkla başlar. Sabah namazının vakti ve oruç bu anda başlar; oruç tutan kişi yeme içmeyi gösterilen vakitten önce bırakmalıdır.
Sabah namazının vakti imsâkla başlar ve güneş doğunca sona erer. Bu sonraki Sabâh işareti ihtiyatlı bir takvim tavsiyesidir; ikinci bir fecir değildir.
Güneş vakti sabah namazı süresini bitirir ve kerâhet süresini başlatır. Uyarı, güneş İşrak seviyesine yükselinceye kadar devam eder.
İşrak, güneşin ufuktan belirgin biçimde yükselmesiyle doğuş kerâhetinin sona erdiğini gösterir. Bundan sonra nafile kuşluk namazı kılınabilir.
Dahve-i Kübrâ, imsâk ile akşam arasındaki şer‘î gündüzün yarısıdır. Hanefî fıkhında bazı oruçlara niyet edilebilecek son zamanla ilgilidir.
Kırmızı uyarı, güneşin en yüksek noktadan geçtiği kısa zeval süresini gösterir. Süre bitip öğle vakti girinceye kadar namaza başlanmamalıdır.
Öğle, güneş meridyeni geçip gölgeler yeniden uzamaya başlayınca girer. Seçilen mezhebin ikindi sınırına kadar devam eder.
Bu, Şâfiî, Mâlikî ve Hanbelî mezhepleriyle Hanefîlerden Ebû Yûsuf ve Muhammed’in kullandığı bir gölge boyu ikindi sınırıdır.
İki gölge boyu esasına dayanan bu sonraki ikindi sınırı İmâm-ı Âzam Ebû Hanîfe’ye nispet edilir. Ayrı bir namaz değildir.
İsfirâr güneş sararıp batmaya yaklaşınca başlar. İkindiyi mazeretsiz geciktirmeyin; kılınmadıysa farzı güneş batmadan eda edin.
Akşam, güneş tamamen battığında başlar ve geçerli yatsı şafak sınırına kadar sürer. Namazın vaktin başında kılınması tercih edilir.
İştibâk, yıldızların belirgin biçimde çoğaldığı takvim işaretidir. Akşam namazını mazeretsiz bu kadar geciktirmemeye dair uyarıdır; ayrı namaz değildir.
İlk yatsı işareti batıdaki kızıllık kaybolunca girer. Üç Sünnî mezhep ile Hanefîlerden Ebû Yûsuf ve Muhammed bu sınırı kullanır.
İşâ-i sânî, batıdaki kalan beyazlık kaybolunca giren ve İmâm-ı Âzam Ebû Hanîfe’ye nispet edilen sonraki yatsı sınırıdır.
Şer‘î gece yarısı, akşamla ertesi imsâk arasının ortasıdır; her zaman saat 00.00 değildir. Yatsıyı geciktirme hükümleriyle ilgilidir.
Teheccüd nafile gece namazıdır. Takvim, dua ve istiğfar için kıymetli olan şer‘î gecenin son üçte birinin başlangıcını gösterir.
Seher, şer‘î gecenin imsâktan önceki son altıda biridir. Dua, zikir, istiğfar ve oruç öncesi sahur için değerli bir vakittir.
Kıble saati, güneşin kıble doğrultusuyla hesaplanan hizalanmasını kullanır. Ön, sağ, sol veya arka talimatını izleyin; güneşe doğrudan bakmayın.
